Handling data in RStudio

Author

Carlo Zampieri

This tutorial gives you an example on how you can access and extract data from the files you download from the CMEMS. All the data mentioned here are available in the examples_data folder of the GitHub repository.

The NetCDF-4 format

The files you download from Copernicus are often in the format NetCDF-4. As described its official documentation, “NetCDF is a set of software libraries and self-describing, machine-independent data formats that support the creation, access, and sharing of array-oriented scientific data”. Imagine NetCDF-4 as a multidimensional array (usually 3D) of data. In the case of the geo-referenced data you download from Copernicus, the array has 3 dimensions: two for longitude and latitude, and one for time or depth, or the combination of them. Common office software don’t work with this format, but programming (R, Python, Matlab, etc.) and GIS (QGIS or ArcGIS) software allow to access and handle NetCDF-4 with great potential. Let’s see some example in RStudio to understand it better!

Useful packages

To work with NetCDF files we need to load some packages which contain useful functions:

library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
library(terra)
library(sf)
Note

See the pre-workshop slides to know how to install the required packages.

Load and explore CMEMS data

For this tutorial we will use data that were downloaded form CMEMS. Particularly, we will use monthly data of surface temperature, salinity and concentration of chlorophyll available in the products Mediterranean Sea Physics Reanalysis and Mediterranean Sea Biogeochemistry Reanalysis.

We use the function list.files() to list the files in the folder examples_data, which present the word cmems in their names:

cmems_files <- list.files("../examples_data/",full.names = T,pattern = "cmems")
cmems_files
[1] "../examples_data/cmems_mod_med_bgc-plankton_my_4.2km_P1M-m_1779453504295.nc"
[2] "../examples_data/cmems_mod_med_phy-sal_my_4.2km_P1M-m_1779453175516.nc"     
[3] "../examples_data/cmems_mod_med_phy-temp_my_4.2km_P1M-m_1779453289660.nc"

There are 3 files, one for each of the variables. We use the function rast from the terra package to load the files in RStudio as one object of class SpatRaster:

cmems_data <- rast(cmems_files)
cmems_data
class       : SpatRaster 
dimensions  : 108, 180, 12  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 0.04166668, 0.04166665  (x, y)
extent      : 11.47917, 18.97917, 41.5, 46  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (CRS84) (OGC:CRS84) 
sources     : cmems_mod_med_bgc-plankton_my_4.2km_P1M-m_1779453504295.nc  (4 layers) 
              cmems_mod_med_phy-sal_my_4.2km_P1M-m_1779453175516.nc  (4 layers) 
              cmems_mod_med_phy-temp_my_4.2km_P1M-m_1779453289660.nc  (4 layers) 
varnames    : chl (Concentration of Chlorophyll in sea water) 
              so (Salinity) 
              thetao (Potential temperature) 
names       : chl_d~366_1, chl_d~366_2, chl_d~366_3, chl_d~366_4, so_de~366_1, so_de~366_2, ... 
unit        :      mg m-3,      mg m-3,      mg m-3,      mg m-3,       0.001,       0.001, ... 
time        : 2020-06-01 to 2020-09-01 UTC

The SpatRaster object is like a 3D grid. The three dimensions are defined as rows, columns and layers. Rows and columns define a grid of cells across longitude and latitude, respectively. Layers are given by the product between the number of variables, time slices and depth slices. In our case, we have 3 variables (temperature, salinity and concentration of chlorophyll), 4 time slices (the files contain monthly data from June to September 2020), and just 1 depth slice since we are interested in surface variables - hence, we have a total of 12 layers. By calling the cmems_data object in which we loaded the CMEMS files, we get a description of the object features like the spatial and temporal resolution and extent, the variable names, the coordinate system, etc. (see the output above). There are specific functions to access and if necessary modify some of the raster features. varnames() shows the name of the variables. time() shows the time at which each layer refers to. names() shows the layers names.

varnames(cmems_data)
[1] "chl"    "so"     "thetao"
time(cmems_data)
 [1] "2020-06-01 UTC" "2020-07-01 UTC" "2020-08-01 UTC" "2020-09-01 UTC"
 [5] "2020-06-01 UTC" "2020-07-01 UTC" "2020-08-01 UTC" "2020-09-01 UTC"
 [9] "2020-06-01 UTC" "2020-07-01 UTC" "2020-08-01 UTC" "2020-09-01 UTC"
names(cmems_data)
 [1] "chl_depth=1.0182366_1"    "chl_depth=1.0182366_2"   
 [3] "chl_depth=1.0182366_3"    "chl_depth=1.0182366_4"   
 [5] "so_depth=1.0182366_1"     "so_depth=1.0182366_2"    
 [7] "so_depth=1.0182366_3"     "so_depth=1.0182366_4"    
 [9] "thetao_depth=1.0182366_1" "thetao_depth=1.0182366_2"
[11] "thetao_depth=1.0182366_3" "thetao_depth=1.0182366_4"

Note that the layers names include the variable name, the depth slice, and the layer number (for example the first, the second, the third or the forth layer of the file). Layers names can be changed in order to be more informative, for example to show just the variable name and the time slice, as shown in the following box:

names(cmems_data) <- paste(gsub("_.*","",names(cmems_data)),time(cmems_data),sep = '_')
names(cmems_data)
 [1] "chl_2020-06-01"    "chl_2020-07-01"    "chl_2020-08-01"   
 [4] "chl_2020-09-01"    "so_2020-06-01"     "so_2020-07-01"    
 [7] "so_2020-08-01"     "so_2020-09-01"     "thetao_2020-06-01"
[10] "thetao_2020-07-01" "thetao_2020-08-01" "thetao_2020-09-01"

We can also explore the data by plotting them with the function plot():

plot(cmems_data,main=names(cmems_data))

Extract data by location and time

It is common to want to extract the values for specific locations and times or time periods. The sample.csv file in the example_data folder reports a table with date and coordinates of 6 sampling events carried out in the Adriatic Sea. We use the functions read.csv() and head() to load and explore the file, respectively:

sample_xy <- read.csv("../examples_data/sample.csv",dec = ".",sep = ";")
head(sample_xy)
        Date      Lat      Lon
1 14/06/2020 44.99806 12.62444
2 20/06/2020 44.17603 13.12070
3 12/07/2020 45.60828 13.45355
4 26/07/2020 44.12694 12.89472
5 01/08/2020 44.00707 13.19172
6 16/08/2020 45.37222 13.13417

We can even plot the points over one the raster layers:

plot(cmems_data,1,main=names(cmems_data)[1])
points(sample_xy$Lon,sample_xy$Lat,pch=16,add=TRUE)

The extract() function from the terra package allows to search into a raster the values of specific locations (expressed in coordinates):

extract(cmems_data,sample_xy[,c(3,2)])
  ID chl_2020-06-01 chl_2020-07-01 chl_2020-08-01 chl_2020-09-01 so_2020-06-01

  so_2020-07-01 so_2020-08-01 so_2020-09-01 thetao_2020-06-01 thetao_2020-07-01
1      34.97503      36.02798      36.05122          20.55059          24.77812
2      37.15281      37.98838      38.43053          21.89000          25.11073
3      36.84688      36.82774      37.16343          22.46881          25.23509
4      35.96719      36.87722      37.10883          21.98404          25.62411
5      36.35640      37.38656      37.89978          21.80790          25.38047
6      37.59502      37.47272      38.34882          22.23587          24.96291

The function produced a table with the values for each point (rows) from each layer of the cmems_data object (columns). We can transpose the table to have a column for the layer name and one for the extracted values by using the function pivot_longer() (from the tidyr package). We concatenate the executions by using the pipe operator %>% implemented in the dplyr package:

extract(cmems_data,sample_xy[,c(3,2)]) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -1,names_to = "layer",values_to = "value")
# A tibble: 72 × 3
      ID layer              value
   <dbl> <chr>              <dbl>
 1     1 chl_2020-06-01     1.28 
 2     1 chl_2020-07-01     0.944
 3     1 chl_2020-08-01     0.572
 4     1 chl_2020-09-01     0.651
 5     1 so_2020-06-01     34.6  
 6     1 so_2020-07-01     35.0  
 7     1 so_2020-08-01     36.0  
 8     1 so_2020-09-01     36.1  
 9     1 thetao_2020-06-01 20.6  
10     1 thetao_2020-07-01 24.8  
# ℹ 62 more rows

To get a tidier table, we can also split the layer column into variable and date by using the function separate():

extract(cmems_data,sample_xy[,c(3,2)]) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -1,names_to = "layer",values_to = "value") %>%
  separate(layer,into = c("var","Date"),sep = "_")
# A tibble: 72 × 4
      ID var    Date        value
   <dbl> <chr>  <chr>       <dbl>
 1     1 chl    2020-06-01  1.28 
 2     1 chl    2020-07-01  0.944
 3     1 chl    2020-08-01  0.572
 4     1 chl    2020-09-01  0.651
 5     1 so     2020-06-01 34.6  
 6     1 so     2020-07-01 35.0  
 7     1 so     2020-08-01 36.0  
 8     1 so     2020-09-01 36.1  
 9     1 thetao 2020-06-01 20.6  
10     1 thetao 2020-07-01 24.8  
# ℹ 62 more rows

We can take a further step and have a row for each combination of location and date, and a column for each variable. The pivot_wider() function helps with that:

cmems_extr <- extract(cmems_data,sample_xy[,c(3,2)]) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -1,names_to = "layer",values_to = "value") %>%
  separate(layer,into = c("var","Date"),sep = "_") %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(ID,Date),names_from = var,values_from = value)
cmems_extr
# A tibble: 24 × 5
      ID Date          chl    so thetao
   <dbl> <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
 1     1 2020-06-01 1.28    34.6   20.6
 2     1 2020-07-01 0.944   35.0   24.8
 3     1 2020-08-01 0.572   36.0   26.3
 4     1 2020-09-01 0.651   36.1   24.4
 5     2 2020-06-01 0.168   37.4   21.9
 6     2 2020-07-01 0.134   37.2   25.1
 7     2 2020-08-01 0.0971  38.0   26.6
 8     2 2020-09-01 0.113   38.4   24.0
 9     3 2020-06-01 0.362   36.0   22.5
10     3 2020-07-01 0.358   36.8   25.2
# ℹ 14 more rows

At this point, we just need to select only the locations and dates reported in our sample_xy table. To do so, we need to add an ID column and to convert the date format in order to match the columns of the cmems_extr object. We use the mutate() function to modify the sample_xy object and the left_join() function to merge it with the extracted values:

sample_xy2 <- sample_xy %>%
  separate(Date,into = c("day","month","year"),sep = "/") %>% select(-day) %>%
  mutate(ID = 1:nrow(sample_xy),Date = paste(year,month,"01",sep = "-"),.keep = "unused") %>%
  left_join(cmems_extr,by = c("ID","Date"))
sample_xy2
       Lat      Lon ID       Date       chl       so   thetao
1 44.99806 12.62444  1 2020-06-01 1.2820040 34.56345 20.55059
2 44.17603 13.12070  2 2020-06-01 0.1679658 37.40252 21.89000
3 45.60828 13.45355  3 2020-07-01 0.3583637 36.84688 25.23509
4 44.12694 12.89472  4 2020-07-01 0.3323720 35.96719 25.62411
5 44.00707 13.19172  5 2020-08-01 0.1102043 37.38656 26.78592
6 45.37222 13.13417  6 2020-08-01 0.1642492 37.47272 26.35469

Extract data by area

A similar operation can be done also for extracting the mean value of a variable within a certain area. To do so, you need a shapefile of the area (or areas) you are interested in. In the examples_data folder there is the shapefile of 6 random coastal areas of the Adriatic Sea. The vect() function from the terra package allows to load shapefile in RStudio:

sample_area <- vect("../examples_data/coastal_areas.shp")
sample_area
 class       : SpatVector 
 geometry    : polygons 
 dimensions  : 6, 1  (geometries, attributes)
 extent      : 288097.3, 827031.3, 4596486, 5041205  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
 source      : coastal_areas.shp
 coord. ref. : WGS 84 / UTM zone 33N (EPSG:32633) 
 names       :    id
 type        : <chr>
 values      :   a01
                 a02
                 a03

Note that the coordinate reference system (crs) of this object differs form the one of cmems_data. To be able to extract data from the raster, the two objects must have the same crs. We have to re-project sample_areas:

sample_area <- project(sample_area,cmems_data)

Now we can plot them together to see the result:

plot(cmems_data,1,main=names(cmems_data)[1])
plot(sample_area,add=TRUE)

Extracting the mean values for each area is now simple:

extract(cmems_data,sample_area,fun=mean)
  ID chl_2020-06-01 chl_2020-07-01 chl_2020-08-01 chl_2020-09-01 so_2020-06-01
1  1      0.6983162     0.51450707     0.40194512     0.39309711      35.80216

5  5      0.6280028     0.44312886     0.28689974     0.44817816      35.77536
6  6      0.1418689     0.13507093     0.13406739     0.16311606      37.60124
  so_2020-07-01 so_2020-08-01 so_2020-09-01 thetao_2020-06-01 thetao_2020-07-01
1      36.62370      36.56990      37.17688          22.37598          25.51120
2      38.37354      37.98575      38.32849          21.75970          24.47568
3      38.62202      38.79627      38.71707          21.46284          24.61978
4      38.54821      38.60776      38.73978          21.59971          25.02958

6      37.65958      38.09582      38.28213          21.75591          25.46740

By concatenating multiple operations, as we did in the previous section, we can obtain a cleaner table:

cmems_extr_area <- extract(cmems_data,sample_area,fun=mean) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -1,names_to = "layer",values_to = "value") %>%
  separate(layer,into = c("var","Date"),sep = "_") %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(ID,Date),names_from = var,values_from = value)
cmems_extr_area
